lessons.title: Lactic Acid Bacteria: Lactobacillus and Streptococcus Species
lessons.body:
Yogurt is made by two main bacteria: Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. They work as a team. Streptococcus starts first, eating lactose (milk sugar) and making lactic acid. This acid makes the milk thick and sour. Then Lactobacillus takes over, making more acid and flavour compounds. In Africa, you can buy freeze-dried sachets of these bacteria from dairy suppliers in Nairobi, Lagos, or Cairo. A typical sachet contains 1 billion live bacteria per gram. For 1 litre of milk, use 0.1 gram of sachet â about a pinch. If you don't have a sachet, you can use 2 tablespoons of fresh, plain, unsweetened yogurt from a previous batch as a starter. But be careful: after 5 to 7 transfers, the bacteria get weak and may pick up unwanted microbes. So buy new sachets every few months.

These bacteria are called 'lactic acid bacteria' because they produce lactic acid. They are safe to eat â in fact, they are good for you. They grow best at 42â45Â°C. If it's too cold (below 30Â°C), they grow slowly and the yogurt may not set. If it's too hot (above 50Â°C), they die. In many African homes, you can use a clean cooler box with a warm water bottle to keep the temperature steady. Or use a yogurt incubator â a simple box with a light bulb â that many small dairies in Kenya and Uganda use.

You need to keep the milk clean. Boil the milk first to kill other bacteria, then cool it to 45Â°C before adding the starter. If you add starter to hot milk, you kill the good bacteria. Use a thermometer â a simple kitchen thermometer costs less than $5. Stir the starter in well. Then cover and leave for 4 to 6 hours. The yogurt is ready when it thickens and smells slightly sour. Refrigerate immediately to stop the acid from getting too strong. With practice, you will know the right set by looking at the spoon â it should coat the back without running off.

lessons.title: Probiotic Strains and Health Benefits
lessons.body:
Probiotics are live bacteria that give health benefits when you eat them. In yogurt, the main probiotics are Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. But not all yogurt has probiotics. If you heat yogurt after fermentation, the bacteria die â then it's not probiotic. So always choose or make yogurt that has not been heated after culturing. In Africa, many people eat yogurt for stomach problems, diarrhoea, and even to help with lactose intolerance. Research in Nigeria and South Africa shows that regular yogurt eaters have fewer gut infections. That's because good bacteria crowd out bad ones like E. coli and Salmonella.

To get health benefits, you need at least 1 million live bacteria per gram of yogurt. A typical homemade yogurt has 10 to 100 million per gram â plenty. But if you use a starter that only has Streptococcus and no Lactobacillus, you get less probiotic effect. So check your starter sachet â it should list both Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. Some sachets also add Bifidobacterium or Lactobacillus acidophilus. These extra strains survive better in the gut. In Kenya, companies like Bio Foods and Brookside sell probiotic yogurt with added Bifidobacterium. You can also buy probiotic sachets from pharmacies in Lagos or Accra.

For a small business, you can market your yogurt as 'probiotic' if you follow three rules: (1) use a starter with live probiotic strains, (2) do not heat the yogurt after fermentation, and (3) store it cold (below 8Â°C). If you leave yogurt in the sun, the bacteria die and the yogurt spoils. Also, avoid adding too much sugar or artificial flavours before fermentation â they can slow bacterial growth. Instead, add honey or fruit after fermentation. Many African customers believe in the health power of yogurt. You can charge a premium if you explain that your yogurt has live cultures. But never claim it cures diseases â just say it supports digestion. That's honest and keeps you out of trouble with regulators.

lessons.title: Culture Preparation and Maintenance
lessons.body:
To prepare a starter culture, you first need a mother culture. Buy a freeze-dried sachet from a dairy supplier. In Nairobi, you can get it from Davis & Shirtliff or from agrovet shops. In West Africa, try Grand Cereals in Nigeria or local dairy cooperatives. A 1-gram sachet costs about $5 and can make 100 litres of yogurt. To activate it, mix the sachet into 1 litre of sterilised milk at 45Â°C. Stir well, cover, and incubate at 42â45Â°C for 4â6 hours until it sets. This is your mother culture. Then you can use 2 tablespoons of this mother culture to start a new batch of 1 litre. That new batch becomes your working culture.

Maintaining a culture means keeping it alive and clean. Store the mother culture in the fridge (4Â°C) for up to 2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze it in small ice cube trays â each cube is about 1 tablespoon. When you need it, thaw one cube and add to 1 litre of warm milk. But freezing can damage some bacteria. So every 2 months, buy a new sachet to refresh your culture. Never use a culture that smells bad, looks discoloured, or has mold. Also, never use metal spoons â use plastic or stainless steel. Metal ions can kill bacteria. Always work with clean hands and sterilised jars. Boil jars for 10 minutes or wash with bleach solution (1 tablespoon bleach per 1 litre water) and rinse well.

In hot African climates, you must be extra careful. Bacteria grow fast, but so do contaminants. Keep your culture area free of flies and dust. Use a clean cloth to cover jars. If you see gas bubbles or a yeasty smell, throw it out â that's contamination. For small businesses, you can maintain a 'backslop' system: keep 2 tablespoons of yesterday's yogurt as starter for today. But after 5â7 days, the culture gets weak and may taste bitter. So switch to a fresh mother culture every week. Write the date on every jar. That way you know when to refresh. With good care, your culture can last for months and save you money.

lessons.title: Strain Selection for Flavor and Texture
lessons.body:
Different strains of bacteria give different flavours and textures. The classic yogurt strains are Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. But within these species, there are many strains. Some make more acid, some make more aroma. For example, Lactobacillus bulgaricus produces acetaldehyde â that's the fresh, green apple smell of yogurt. Streptococcus thermophilus makes diacetyl â a buttery flavour. If you want a mild yogurt, choose a strain that produces less acid. If you want a tangy yogurt, choose a high-acid strain. In Africa, local yogurts often have a strong, sour taste because they are fermented longer. But many urban customers prefer mild yogurt. So you can select strains to match your market.

Texture also depends on strains. Some bacteria produce exopolysaccharides (EPS) â natural thickeners. Strains that make EPS give a creamy, ropy texture. Others give a firm, gel-like set. If you want a thick yogurt without adding milk powder, choose an EPS-producing strain. For example, certain strains of Streptococcus thermophilus are known for ropiness. You can buy defined strains from culture collections like the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) or from local suppliers who sell 'texture blends'. In Kenya, some dairy suppliers sell a blend called 'YO-MIX' that gives a mild flavour and thick texture. It costs about $10 per sachet but makes 100 litres.

How do you test a new strain? Make a small batch â 1 litre. Ferment for 4 hours, then taste and check texture. Does it set firmly? Is it too sour? Does it smell good? If you like it, scale up. But remember: strains behave differently in different milks. Cow milk, goat milk, and camel milk all have different proteins and fats. Camel milk, common in northern Kenya and Somalia, makes a thinner yogurt. So you may need a strain that produces more EPS. Also, if you add sugar or fruit, the bacteria may produce less acid. So always test with your actual recipe. For a business, consistency is key. Once you find a blend that works, stick with it. Buy from the same supplier and store it properly. That way, your customers get the same taste every time.

lessons.title: Microbial Growth Kinetics in Yogurt
lessons.body:
Microbial growth kinetics is just a fancy way of saying how fast bacteria grow. In yogurt, the bacteria go through four phases: lag, log, stationary, and death. When you first add starter to milk, the bacteria need time to adjust â that's the lag phase. It lasts about 30 minutes to 1 hour. Then they start multiplying fast â the log phase. In this phase, one bacterium divides into two every 20 to 30 minutes. So after 4 hours, you can have millions of bacteria per millilitre. That's when the milk thickens. Then they enter stationary phase, where growth slows because acid builds up. Finally, if you leave it too long, they die â that's the death phase. So you must stop fermentation at the right time.

How do you know when to stop? The pH should be around 4.5 to 4.6. You can buy pH strips for less than $2. Or you can use a simple acid test: titratable acidity. That's the amount of acid in the yogurt. For good yogurt, titratable acidity should be 0.7% to 1.0% lactic acid. You can test this with a kit from a dairy supplier. But for most small producers, taste and texture are enough. When the yogurt coats a spoon and tastes mildly sour, it's ready. In hot climates, fermentation is faster. At 45Â°C, it may take only 3 hours. At 40Â°C, it may take 5 hours. So always check every 30 minutes after the first 3 hours.

Temperature control is critical. If the temperature drops below 40Â°C, the bacteria grow slowly and you may get a weak set. If it goes above 50Â°C, they die. In many African homes, people use a warm water bath: put the yogurt container in a larger pot with water at 45Â°C. Cover with a blanket. Or use a cooler box with a hot water bottle. For a small business, invest in an incubator. A simple wooden box with a 40-watt light bulb and a thermostat costs about $50 and can hold 20 litres. That gives you consistent results. Also, the starting number of bacteria matters. If you add too little starter, the lag phase is longer and contaminants may grow. So use the recommended amount: 0.1 gram per litre of freeze-dried starter, or 2 tablespoons of fresh yogurt per litre. Never guess â measure.

lessons.title: Preventing Phage Contamination in Starter Cultures
lessons.body:
Phages are viruses that attack bacteria. They are everywhere â in soil, water, and even in the air. In yogurt production, phages can kill your starter bacteria, and then the milk won't ferment. You'll end up with a sweet, runny liquid instead of yogurt. This is a big problem in dairies. In Africa, phage outbreaks have shut down small yogurt businesses. So you must prevent them. How do phages get in? They come from raw milk, dust, dirty equipment, and even from the air. Once they are in your culture, they multiply fast and can wipe out your starter in one batch.

To prevent phages, you need strict hygiene. First, always use pasteurised or boiled milk. Raw milk carries phages. Second, sanitise everything that touches the culture: jars, spoons, thermometers, and your hands. Use a bleach solution (1 tablespoon per litre of water) or a commercial sanitiser. Third, never leave your culture open to the air. Cover it with a clean lid. Fourth, use a closed system if possible. For example, some small dairies use a 'phage barrier' â they rotate between different starter strains. Phages are specific: a phage that attacks Streptococcus thermophilus won't attack Lactobacillus bulgaricus. So if you alternate strains every few days, phages can't build up. Fifth, keep a backup culture in the freezer. If your working culture fails, you can start fresh from the backup.

Another trick is to use a 'starter rotation' schedule. For example, use Strain A for Monday and Tuesday, Strain B for Wednesday and Thursday, and Strain C for Friday and Saturday. This prevents phages from adapting to one strain. Also, avoid using the same room for handling raw milk and for culturing. If you must, do the culturing first, then handle raw milk. And always clean up spills immediately. In Kenya, some dairy cooperatives have a separate 'clean room' for starter handling. You can do the same with a small plastic tent or a clean cupboard. If you suspect a phage attack â the yogurt doesn't set, or it sets then turns runny â throw out the culture and start with a new sachet. Don't try to save it. Phages are tough. But with good hygiene and rotation, you can keep them out and keep your yogurt business running.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Starter Cultures and Fermentation Microbiology for African Yogurt Enterprises

For small and medium yogurt businesses across Africa, the starter culture is not a laboratory curiosity â it is the engine of your production line, your quality control department, and your brand identity all at once. Whether you are fermenting in Kano, Kisumu, or Kampala, the microbiology of Lactobacillus and Streptococcus determines your yield, shelf life, texture, and repeat-customer rate. This practical reference consolidates the working knowledge you need to select, prepare, maintain, and protect starter cultures under real African production conditions â variable ambient temperatures, intermittent power, and limited cold-chain infrastructure.

Why Fermentation Microbiology Is a Business Issue

Every failed batch is lost revenue. A phage-contaminated vat can wipe out a day's milk purchase. An over-acidified culture produces whey separation that customers read as "spoiled." A weak culture means thin yogurt that competes poorly against imported brands. Understanding the biology lets you diagnose problems in hours rather than discarding entire production runs. In markets where fresh milk is expensive and margins are thin, culture management is the single highest-leverage technical skill a yogurt enterprise can develop.

Understanding the Two Core Organisms

Traditional yogurt fermentation relies on a symbiotic relationship between Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus. S. thermophilus grows first, producing lactic acid and consuming oxygen, which creates the anaerobic, acidic environment that L. bulgaricus needs. In turn, L. bulgaricus releases amino acids and peptides from milk proteins that stimulate S. thermophilus growth. This mutualism is why the pair acidifies milk far faster together than either does alone â typically reaching pH 4.5 in 3â5 hours at 42â45 Â°C.

For African producers without reliable incubation rooms, this temperature sensitivity matters. Below 38 Â°C, S. thermophilus dominates and the yogurt is mild but slow to set. Above 46 Â°C, L. bulgaricus dominates and the product becomes sharply acidic with a pronounced acetaldehyde aroma. Many Kenyan and Nigerian processors use insulated boxes, water baths, or even repurposed coolers with warm water to hold 42â45 Â°C â a practical workaround worth documenting in your SOP.

Probiotic Strains: A Premium Positioning Opportunity

Adding Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Lactobacillus acidophilus, or Bifidobacterium spp. allows you to market "probiotic yogurt" at a 20â40 % price premium in urban African markets. However, probiotics require viable counts of at least 10â¶ CFU/g at end of shelf life. Because L. bulgaricus continues acidifying during cold storage, it can kill off added probiotics. The practical solution is to add probiotic strains after fermentation, just before packaging, or to use a mild post-fermentation cooling regime (below 6 Â°C within 2 hours). Document viable counts with periodic lab testing if you make health claims.

Data Table 1: Growth and Acidification Parameters

Table 1. Key growth parameters for yogurt starter organisms
Parameter S. thermophilus L. bulgaricus Practical implication
Optimal growth temp.40â45 Â°C42â47 Â°CTarget 42â45 Â°C for balanced flavor
Acid tolerance (min. pH)~4.2~3.8L. bulgaricus drives over-acidification
Primary acid producedL(+)-lactic acidD(â)-lactic acidL(+) is more easily metabolized by humans
Flavor compoundDiacetyl (buttery)Acetaldehyde (green apple)Ratio determines sensory profile
Generation time (42 Â°C)~25 min~40 minExplains why S. thermophilus leads early
Oxygen requirementFacultative anaerobeAnaerobe (aerotolerant)Closed vats improve both

Source: Tamime & Robinson, Yoghurt: Science and Technology, 3rd ed. (Woodhead, 2007); FAO/WHO Codex Standard for Fermented Milks (CXS 243-2003).

Culture Preparation and Maintenance

Working cultures should be prepared by inoculating sterile reconstituted skim milk (10â12 % solids) with a freeze-dried or frozen commercial starter, then incubating at 42 Â°C until a firm coagulum forms. This "mother culture" is then used at 1â3 % to inoculate bulk production milk. Never carry a culture more than 15â20 generations â over time, phage resistance erodes, acid production drifts, and contaminants accumulate. For African SMEs without a microbiology lab, the safest approach is to purchase commercial direct-vat-set (DVS) cultures and use them for 5â10 back-slopping cycles maximum before buying fresh stock.

If you must maintain a frozen stock, glycerol at 10â15 % v/v in a â20 Â°C freezer (or â80 Â°C if available) preserves viability for 3â6 months. Where grid power is unreliable, a backup generator or a solar-powered freezer is a business-critical investment â losing a master culture can halt production for a week.

Data Table 2: Culture Format Trade-offs for African SMEs

Table 2. Starter culture formats compared
Format Storage Cost per 100 L Best for
Freeze-dried DVSAmbient (cool, dry)MediumMost African SMEs; no freezer needed
Frozen pelletsâ18 Â°C or colderLowâmediumProducers with reliable cold chain
Freeze-dried bulk powderAmbientLowLarge dairies with lab support
Back-slopped working culture4â8 Â°CVery lowDaily production; max 5â10 cycles
Mother culture (frozen)â20 Â°CLowCost control with freezer access

Source: Danisco/Chr. Hansen technical bulletins on yogurt cultures; ILRI dairy value chain training materials (Nairobi).

Strain Selection for Flavor and Texture

Strain choice is a marketing decision as much as a technical one. Exopolysaccharide (EPS)-producing strains yield thicker, creamier yogurt with less whey separation â a major advantage in markets where consumers judge quality visually. Mild strains suit children's products and urban supermarkets; high-acetaldehyde strains suit traditional sour-milk palates familiar with mala, amasi, or laban. Test 2â3 commercial blends against your target customer segment before committing to a bulk purchase.

Microbial Growth Kinetics in Practice

Yogurt fermentation follows a standard bacterial growth curve: lag (0â30 min), exponential (30 minâ3 h), stationary (3â5 h), and death phase. Your job is to stop fermentation at the start of stationary phase â when pH reaches 4.5â4.6 â by rapid cooling. In hot African climates, passive cooling is insufficient; you need active refrigeration or an ice-water bath. Delayed cooling is the most common cause of over-acid, whey-separated yogurt in small enterprises.

Preventing Phage Contamination

Bacteriophages are viruses that infect starter bacteria and can destroy a culture's acidifying ability within a single batch. They are the single most feared problem in industrial dairy fermentation. Phage build-up occurs when the same strain is used repeatedly in the same facility, when whey aerosols spread through the air, or when sanitation is incomplete. Rotating between 2â3 phage-unrelated commercial cultures every few weeks is the standard defence.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Phage and Pathogen Control

Never reuse whey or yogurt from a failed or slow-acidifying batch as inoculum â it is likely phage-contaminated and will infect your next production run. Never handle raw milk and finished yogurt with the same utensils. Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella, and E. coli O157:H7 can survive in improperly pasteurized milk and cause serious illness. Pasteurize milk to at least 85 Â°C for 5 minutes (or 95 Â°C for 1 minute), sanitize all vats and pipes with peracetic acid or chlorine-based sanitisers, and keep fermentation rooms separate from raw-milk receiving areas. If you suspect phage, discard the culture, deep-clean the entire line, and switch to a different commercial strain.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Pasteurize milk to â¥85 Â°C for 5 min; cool to 42â45 Â°C before inoculation.
  2. Use 1â3 % v/v active starter; verify activity with a small pre-batch if uncertain.
  3. Hold incubation at 42â45 Â°C; check pH or coagulation every 30 minutes after 3 hours.
  4. Stop fermentation at pH 4.5â4.6; cool to <8 Â°C within 2 hours.
  5. Rotate between 2â3 phage-unrelated commercial cultures every 2â4 weeks.
  6. Limit back-slopping to 5â10 generations; then buy fresh DVS stock.
  7. Sanitize all contact surfaces; never mix raw milk tools with finished product tools.
  8. Record batch number, culture lot, pH, and incubation time for every production run.

Further Reading

  • FAO/WHO â Codex Standard for Fermented Milks (CXS 243-2003)
  • FAO â Fermented Dairy Products resource page
  • ILRI â Dairy value chain and smallholder processing resources (Nairobi)
  • WHO/FAO â Guidelines for the Evaluation of Probiotics in Food
  • FAO â Milk and Dairy Products in Human Nutrition (free PDF)

Business takeaway: Your starter culture is a strategic asset. Treat it with the same discipline you apply to your cash flow â source it reliably, rotate it deliberately, protect it from contamination, and document every batch. Enterprises that master fermentation microbiology consistently produce better yogurt at lower cost, and that is what wins repeat customers in competitive African dairy markets.

quiz.q: Which two bacteria are the main starters for yogurt?
options: A) Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus
quiz.explanation: These two are the classic yogurt cultures.

quiz.q: At what temperature do yogurt starter bacteria grow best?
quiz.explanation: 42â45Â°C is the optimal range for Lactobacillus and Streptococcus.

quiz.q: What is the role of Streptococcus thermophilus in yogurt fermentation?
options: A) It produces lactic acid first and lowers pH
C) It kills all other bacteria
D) It makes the yogurt sweet
quiz.explanation: Streptococcus starts acid production, then Lactobacillus takes over.

quiz.q: How much freeze-dried starter is needed for 1 litre of milk?
quiz.explanation: 0.1 gram (a pinch) is the standard dose for 1 litre.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using metal spoons with starter cultures?
options: A) Metal spoons are too expensive
B) Metal ions can kill bacteria
C) Metal spoons make the yogurt taste metallic
D) Metal spoons are not clean
quiz.explanation: Metal ions can be toxic to lactic acid bacteria.

quiz.q: What is a probiotic?
options: A) A live bacteria that gives health benefits
B) A chemical that preserves yogurt
D) A virus that attacks bacteria
quiz.explanation: Probiotics are live microorganisms with health benefits when consumed.

quiz.q: How many live bacteria per gram should probiotic yogurt have at minimum?
quiz.explanation: At least 1 million CFU per gram is needed for probiotic effect.

quiz.q: Which of these kills probiotic bacteria in yogurt?
quiz.explanation: Heating after fermentation kills the live bacteria.

quiz.q: What is a mother culture?
options: A) The first batch made from a freeze-dried sachet
B) The yogurt you buy from a shop
C) A culture that has been frozen for years
D) A culture that contains only yeast
quiz.explanation: Mother culture is the initial activated culture from a sachet.

quiz.q: How long can you store a mother culture in the fridge?
quiz.explanation: Refrigerated mother culture lasts up to 2 weeks.

quiz.q: Why should you refresh your starter culture every few months?
options: A) Because bacteria get weak and may pick up contaminants
B) Because the culture becomes too sweet
C) Because the culture turns into yeast
D) Because the culture becomes too thick
quiz.explanation: After multiple transfers, bacteria weaken and contamination risk rises.

quiz.q: What is backslop?
options: A) Using a previous batch of yogurt as starter
B) Adding milk powder to yogurt
quiz.explanation: Backslop means saving some yogurt to start the next batch.

quiz.q: Which compound gives yogurt its fresh, green apple smell?
quiz.explanation: Acetaldehyde is produced by Lactobacillus bulgaricus.

quiz.q: What does EPS stand for in yogurt texture?
quiz.explanation: Exopolysaccharides are natural thickeners produced by some strains.

quiz.q: Why might camel milk make thinner yogurt than cow milk?
options: A) Camel milk has different proteins and fats
B) Camel milk is always sour
C) Camel milk has more sugar
D) Camel milk is not pasteurised
quiz.explanation: Camel milk composition affects texture, often requiring EPS-producing strains.

quiz.q: What is the lag phase in microbial growth?
options: A) When bacteria are adjusting and not yet multiplying
C) When bacteria are growing fastest
D) When bacteria are forming spores
quiz.explanation: Lag phase is the adaptation period before rapid growth.

quiz.q: During log phase, how often do yogurt bacteria divide?
quiz.explanation: Under optimal conditions, they double every 20â30 minutes.

quiz.q: What is the ideal pH for stopping yogurt fermentation?
quiz.explanation: pH 4.5â4.6 gives good set and flavour.

quiz.q: What is titratable acidity in yogurt?
options: A) The amount of acid in the yogurt
B) The amount of sugar in the yogurt
C) The amount of protein in the yogurt
D) The amount of fat in the yogurt
quiz.explanation: It measures the total acid, ideally 0.7%â1.0% lactic acid.

quiz.q: Why is temperature control critical during fermentation?
options: A) Too cold slows growth, too hot kills bacteria
B) Temperature does not affect bacteria
C) Cold temperatures make yogurt too sour
D) Hot temperatures make yogurt sweeter
quiz.explanation: Bacteria are sensitive to temperature extremes.

quiz.q: What is a phage?
options: A) A virus that attacks bacteria
B) A type of good bacteria
quiz.explanation: Phages are viruses that infect and kill bacteria.

quiz.q: What happens if phages contaminate your starter?
options: B) The yogurt does not set and stays runny
quiz.explanation: Phages kill starter bacteria, preventing fermentation.

quiz.q: How can you prevent phage contamination?
options: B) Leave cultures open to air
C) Sanitise all equipment and use pasteurised milk
quiz.explanation: Hygiene and pasteurisation reduce phage entry.

quiz.q: What is starter rotation?
options: A) Alternating different starter strains to prevent phage buildup
B) Spinning the starter in a centrifuge
quiz.explanation: Rotation prevents phages from adapting to one strain.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a backup culture in the freezer?
options: A) To have a fresh start if the working culture fails
B) To make the yogurt sweeter
D) To save money on milk
quiz.explanation: Backup ensures you can recover from contamination or failure.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of phage contamination?
options: B) Yogurt sets then turns runny
quiz.explanation: Phages cause failed or weak set, often after initial thickening.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect phage contamination?
options: A) Throw out the culture and start with a new sachet
B) Add more milk and hope for the best
C) Heat the culture to kill phages
D) Add sugar to mask the problem
quiz.explanation: Phages are hard to eliminate; start fresh with new starter.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a good practice for starter maintenance?
options: B) Storing mother culture in the fridge
C) Using the same culture for months without refreshing
quiz.explanation: Cultures weaken over time and should be refreshed regularly.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amount of fresh yogurt to use as starter for 1 litre of milk?
quiz.explanation: 2 tablespoons of fresh yogurt per litre is a common ratio.

quiz.q: Why is it important to cool boiled milk to 45Â°C before adding starter?
options: A) To avoid killing the bacteria with heat
B) To make the milk thicker
quiz.explanation: Temperatures above 50Â°C can kill starter bacteria.
